```{r, include = FALSE}
has_ggplot2 <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
has_patchwork <- requireNamespace("patchwork", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 4.2,
  eval = has_ggplot2
)
```

RdistNN ships ggplot2-based views of fitted local estimators. ggplot2 (and,
for dashboards, patchwork) are suggested dependencies: everything in this
vignette degrades with an actionable message when they are missing, and
every panel is a regular ggplot object that can be extended with `+`.

The running example is a CATE fit with oracle nuisance columns, evaluated
along a profile in the first covariate.

```{r fit}
library(RdistNN)

set.seed(42)
n <- 400
X <- cbind(X1 = runif(n, -2, 2), X2 = rnorm(n))
e <- plogis(0.4 * X[, "X1"])
tau <- 1 + sin(X[, "X1"])
m0 <- X[, "X1"] - 0.5 * X[, "X2"]
treat <- as.integer(runif(n) < e)
Y <- m0 + treat * tau + rnorm(n, sd = 0.5)

df <- data.frame(X, T = treat, Y = Y, e = e, m0 = m0, m1 = m0 + tau)
X0 <- cbind(X1 = seq(-1.5, 1.5, length.out = 11), X2 = 0)

fit <- cate_dnn(
  data = df, x_cols = c("X1", "X2"), y_col = "Y", t_col = "T",
  e_col = "e", m0_col = "m0", m1_col = "m1",
  X0 = X0, k = 1L, se = TRUE, jackknife = "fast",
  return = c("W", "dx")
)
```

## The estimate panel

`plot()` (equivalently `ggplot2::autoplot()`, or `plot_estimates()` with
more options) draws the profile with jackknife confidence bounds, a zero
reference line, and the honesty caption: the median effective sample size
across targets and the kernel order `s` with its provenance — here the
default paper rule, since neither `s` nor `tuning` was supplied.

```{r estimates}
plot(fit)
```

Small non-profile target sets render as a forest layout with labels built
from the stored coordinates, and `style =`/`x_var =` override the
automatic choices.

## Weight geometry

The weight panels show what the estimator averaged over. The effective
kernel view is the most instructive: DNN weights as a data-driven kernel
in distance space, with the rank-`s` radius marked.

```{r weights-kernel}
plot_weights(fit, type = "kernel", targets = 6L)
```

```{r weights-cumulative}
plot_weights(fit, type = "cumulative", targets = c(1L, 6L, 11L))
```

## Overlap diagnostics

For CATE fits, `plot_overlap()` shows whether both treatment arms carry
weight near each target. With simplex weights the treated and control
masses partition one, so the treated mass is the local treated share;
shaded bands mark shares outside `share_limits`.

```{r overlap-mass}
plot_overlap(fit, type = "mass")
```

The propensity view draws the weighted propensity distribution at
selected targets when observation-level propensities are available (as
here, through `e_col`), and a weighted q10–q90 summary otherwise.

```{r overlap-propensity}
plot_overlap(fit, type = "propensity", targets = c(1L, 6L, 11L))
```

## Weight diagnostics facets

`autoplot()` on a `diagnostics()` frame tracks the effective sample size
(with the degenerate-weights guide at `0.9 n`), the maximum weight, and
the top-5 weight share across targets.

```{r diagnostics}
ggplot2::autoplot(diagnostics(fit))
```

## The dashboard

`plot_dashboard()` composes the panels with a metadata annotation. It
requires patchwork; without it the panels are returned as a named list.
Panels whose inputs are unavailable are substituted rather than failing
the dashboard — a matrix-interface fit without stored treatment gets the
diagnostics facets in place of the overlap panel.

```{r dashboard, eval = has_ggplot2 && has_patchwork, fig.height = 8}
plot_dashboard(fit)
```

## Customising panels

Every builder returns a plain ggplot object; add layers, scales, or a
different theme as usual.

```{r custom}
plot_estimates(fit, level = 0.9) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "CATE profile, 90% intervals") +
  ggplot2::theme_classic(base_size = 11)
```

For fully custom figures, the tidy frames behind the panels are exported:
`plot_data_estimates()`, `plot_data_weights()`, and
`plot_data_diagnostics()`.
